en: Praise from the Feet to the Hair of Śiva's Head ॥

May that Lord of Mountains always bestow auspiciousness upon you—the mountain where the heroic deeds of Rudra are sung by the wives of the hosts of Vidyādharas absorbed in play within the bowers of the Kalpa-grove shimmering on its slopes; where the peacocks cry out with loud, resonant notes like the cries of Hari and Ambā, causing the stars to tremble in their sound; and which is the birthplace of Śarva’s bliss. They declare his true nature to be the union of the entire essence of all the gods.

May that Śrī-Pināka, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, who has become the arrow for subduing [the wicked] and is ever-vigilant in protecting the worlds; who is the sovereign even over those who make the earth difficult to traverse;
and who has the three Vedas as His target—may He protect us incessantly from all inauspiciousness.

He who steals away the momentum of the [enemy's] weapons, whose sword-blade is stained by the streams of blood flowing from the throats of hosts of fierce Daityas such as Mātaṅga, and who, though cruel, spreads his own defeat even before ten thousand suns; he who is the refuge for the lotus-feet of all the gods.

May the axe of terrible form, which cleaves for us the dense forest known as our most stubborn sins—[the axe] that has made its dwelling upon the tip of the hand of the Enemy of Time (Śiva), which has been sharpened on the whetstone of the chests of his enemies, and which from time to time is smeared with the oil of affection by the Daughter of the Preeminent Mountain (Pārvatī);

may that trident, whose mouth is the friend of the spreading flames of fire, the absolute destroyer of sin, whose sole nature is to protect those whose hearts are devoted to the service of the feet of Śrī (Umā), protect us! (3–4)

May that hand of the Lord, which bears the deer-mark, grant you well-being— that very hand of the moon-crested God which, as if desiring to master the exceedingly vast expanse of the glances from the corners of the eyes of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) who rests upon his chest, constantly and with great reverence holds within its own interior the joy of the deer through its perpetually elevated digits.

[And may he grant it] whose throat-region is filled with the unimpeded, terrible sounds of the great golden bells attached to its borders, and with the loud cries from his throat that fill the entire space of the cosmic circle.

May the eternal Lord of Elephants, whose tusks are fierce and uplifted, who has swallowed the lofty peaks of Mount Kailāsa like a morsel of *kakubha* fruit, and who is the mount of Time (Kāla) upon his neck, destroy all misfortune.

May the elephant-faced son of Śarvāṇī grant you well-being— he whose broad body resembles a mountain of gold, who removes all obstacles, and who fills the hundreds of caves on the peaks of Śiva’s mountain with the loud humming of swarms of bees made restless by the fragrance of the streams of ichor flowing from his temples.

May that enemy of Tāraka—who, through the merits of the gods, was born as the singular hero Śiva by the consent of Śivā; who, when his name is heard, causes the hosts of Daitya warriors to succumb to a burden of fear;

who split the Krauñca mountain with the tip of his sharpened arrow; and who delivers one from the bottomless well of saṃsāra—may he grant us prosperity. Clad in blue garments, holding in the palm of his hand a bow with an arrow upon it, he rides a horse of towering height that has surpassed the wind with its intense speed.

May the Lord of Beings, who strikes fear into the multitudes of wild beasts such as passion and hatred, sport in the hunt within the forest of my mind. (9) May this indescribable wealth of Śambhu—the enemy of Śambara—be for our prosperity; it is a treasure rendered fit for no other enjoyment than his own, fashioned from two lotuses, two plantain stems, two elephant trunks, two frontal globes of lordly elephants, two tusks of the king of mountains, two conchs, two coral branches, two blue lotuses, and even a cloud, all combined to produce a magnificent splendor. (10)

I worship the crimson life-breaths of the Moon-crested Lord, which have surpassed the graceful play of the beautiful braid of Yamunā (the daughter of the Sun) through the splendor of their own braids; which possess the resonant sounds of noble lutes held in palms that have cast aside the power of Sarasvatī’s speech; and whose outer corners of the eyes are expert at eclipsing the flickering glances of the doe-eyed maidens, appearing like fresh sprouts of *suṣumā* stalks.
In the commencement of dances, Nandin brings joy to the hearts of the assembly with the exceedingly loud sounds of his hand-beaten drum, which utterly surpasses the thundering of clouds.

May Caṇḍīśa and the other lords of the Pramathas—whose majesty is intent upon the excellence of honoring their Master, who is animated by a multitude of fourfold virtues—not be contented [with lesser things].

May the abode of the Lord of the World, whose crest is the crescent moon, be dear to me: a place worthy of being beheld with its great *sāla* trees entwined by nets of pearls and rubies; surrounded on all sides by mansions for the world-protectors set with priceless gems; and encompassed by gardens that are honored by the women of the Mountain-Daughter’s retinue—a dwelling praised by the gods.

Always well-pleased, he [Śiva] is worthy of the veneration of all the sages; his presence is honored by the assembly of all the munis. His side-regions are adorned with pillars fashioned from the finest jewels, and his path of auspicious stairs is inlaid with clusters of pure gems. With beautiful pitchers made of spotless gold, perfectly fashioned upon his head, he possesses a full splendor.
Placed in the center of the assembly hall, he is delightful with footstools shining around him, charming with four feet made of gold and jewels, and radiant in his lofty self.
May the pair of Śiva’s feet, worthy of being dwelt upon at will by the Goddess who has forgotten her own throne due to some incomparably soft and fragrant cloth, bring an end to our suffering.

(15) May those two symmetrical feet of the Lord of the three worlds protect us—feet that rest upon a footstool when He is seated on His throne; whose soles possess the expansive beauty of lotuses and shine with lotus-like markings;
and which are made radiant by the ten toes that glow red from the rows of beautiful diamonds sparkling in the crowns of the gods bowing before Him. (16)
May those two anklets— which proclaim through the voice of the Vedas the entire definition of the peacock’s crest, which produce the bliss of Lakṣmī’s enjoyment upon their forms,
which possess lofty beauty through their association with Śambhu’s worshipful lotus feet, and which bestow all happiness— fulfill our complete auspiciousness.
When the moth-like enemy suddenly met his end in the fire of her eyes— the very source of passion— what is this pair of quivers that has been drawn from him and placed before me?

May that pair of beautiful shanks of the Lord of All, which with their speed could shatter the assembly of gods bowing in fear and the mass of cruel obstacles, remove our accumulated sins from birth after birth.

May those two thighs of the Lord—shining together with his pair of knees, which resemble the ocean of the king of fish (the dolphin-bannered god), and worthy of being compared to royal plantain trees, elephant trunks, or golden pillars; and which partake in the bliss of being gently pressed by the lotus-hand of Gaurī—drive away the long-accumulated evil of our past lives.

My mind ever dances before the hips of the Lord of the Entire World, who bears the crescent moon as his crest; hips which are embraced by a beautiful golden girdle clasped by hands holding clusters of priceless gems; which are draped in a silken garment of Chinese silk that steals the brilliance of a mass of milk; and which manifest the ripening of the virtuous deeds of the Daughter of the Mountain.

[20] [He is adorned] with a waist-band of deep yellow hue, like a ripe mango, tightly bound with a smooth-colored cloth polished by time, and possessing the luster of the sun reddened at the hour of twilight.

May that noble line of hair on the belly of the Enemy of Manmatha—whose greatness is augmented by its own radiant self-luminosity, which is ever engaged in the pursuit of the unreal objects [of worldly desire], and which is auspicious—grant me constant association with blessings.

May that exquisite line of hair, which rises from the basin-like navel-circle surrounded by the beauty of ever-fresh loveliness, which emerges first and then proceeds across the abdomen toward the chest, and which shines intensely like a script proclaiming the meaning of the arrival of Kāma, grant me perpetual joy. It is the crest-jewel of all beautiful things.

May the chest of the Enemy of Dakṣa—beautifully radiant with the luster of newly strung gem necklaces; possessing a noble charm that rivals the rising splendor of the sun due to its contact with the saffron paste smeared upon the firm slopes of the breasts of the Daughter of the Mountain during their embrace; agitated by the Goddess as she quivers on his left lap, her lovely red lotus hand shining against it; and ever-skilled in protecting those who constantly offer him prostrations—protect us. [And] one [hand], busy massaging the peak of the breast of his beloved on his left side, which shines with a beautiful red lotus held in her palm...
We behold the other three exceedingly noble arms of the one whose head is the ocean— adorned with excellent axes and deer, and graced with bound golden armlets and jeweled bracelets.

May that throat of the Blue-Necked One (Śiva) pacify for us the entire mass of calamities— that throat wherein the heat of the Hālāhala poison experiences a state like that of the son of Triśaṅku, due to the forceful driving of both his chariot-steeds by Viṣṇu, who was himself agitated by the fear of his wife’s widowhood and distressed by the suffering of all the worlds.

May this lip-jewel of the newborn bestow upon us a collection of riches— a lip marked by the tender tooth-prints of the Daughter of the Mountain King, blended with the extreme whiteness of her radiant teeth,
shining with a luster resembling a confluence of pearls and rubies.
[This verse describes the lip as being like the pericarp of a golden lotus, shimmering amidst the mass of light from various jewels in her ear-ornaments.]
May this mind of ours always, with ease, establish itself upon the two feet of Śambhu—the wind that fans the lotus-heart of those who bow to him—while directing its nose toward the [divine] nose.

May those two earrings of yours, which surpass the best of elephants, bring us prosperity; they hang from the lobes of your ears like a pair of golden [lotuses], shining intensely through contact with excellent gems of most beautiful luster, clearly outshining the spreading radiance of the rising sun, and serving as the writing-tablet for the record of birth and death worn upon the foreheads of the rows of your devotees.

I offer my salutation with folded palms to those three eyes of the Three-eyed Lord (Śiva)—those through which the divisions of time are established for mortals, who are the mouth of the deities, and whom the best of sages call the "Triad of Deities" (Trayī) in this world—eyes that are like bees ever eager to sport upon the lotus-face of Rudrāṇī, and which have completely drunk away the harshness of the fire born from his forehead. On the left lotus-face of the Goddess seated on his left lap, as she turns toward her beloved, [the eye] drinks up the heat of the fire born from the forehead, leaving nothing behind. Furthermore, [the other two eyes] drink up the various streams of perspiration arising from her.

May the three eyes of the Enemy of Kāma, which are cooled by the intense compassion falling like fire upon the flames of our repeated joy, swiftly remove our threefold suffering. (30) May our heart, free from all internal anxiety, sport in that forehead of the Blue-throated Lord—which acts as a stage for the graceful dance of the most excellent young actress, the playfully flickering eyebrow—wherein the eye shines beautifully like a decorative mark fashioned from saffron powder upon a luster that dispels even the deepest darkness with its moon-like charm. (31)
"O Lord, just as you accepted the Gaṅgā upon your head, please accept me too"—thus entreating the blessed maiden, O Sun, do you not feel compassion for her who is worthy of being burned?

May that Kauśika, who thus generates such doubt among the people, who is exceedingly wealthy, and who possesses the hue of a dark rain-cloud, be exalted for our great welfare, like the Conqueror of Tripura.

[May he be] adorned with garlands of flowers—fit for the ornaments of love, plucked from the hands of the friends of the daughter of the mountain king, and attracting bees by their pervasive fragrance.

May that crown of the Lord, which mocks the peak of the king of mountains—the abode of Murā—with the luster of its rubies, and which is adorned with armor against the multitude of our calamities, dispel our distress.

I salute the charming moon of nectar beautifully fashioned upon the crown of Lord Śambhu; for, though I am crooked in form, blemished, and cold-natured, by the power of serving his feet I have attained the status of an ornament for the Moon-crested Lord, who is easily accessible through his compassion—and thus, even by my own condition, it proclaims: "Let the multitudes of people serve him for their welfare."

May the cool-rayed moon known as the white parasol of the Enemy of Cities (Śiva)—which shines, pervading the universe with its luster as white as a blossoming jasmine flower; which is circular in form and repeatedly bestows supreme bliss upon those who take refuge at its feet; and which is joyfully borne by the hand of Nandin, adorned with jeweled bracelets—may that moon remove all calamities from our feet.
[And may it protect us] from the tremulous side-glances of the excellent companions of Rudrāṇī, who are seated at the sides of Śiva and the Daughter of the Mountain, resplendent in divine ornaments.

May the sweet, resonant tinkling of rows of bracelets and bangles, arising at the moment when the creeper-like arms of the celestial damsels—those most graceful-bodied women devoted to the service of their Lord—swing their chowries as they move, ward off all calamities from us.

(36) I constantly worship the dances of the celestial beauties, whose forms are exquisitely lovely and who are intent on serving their Master; dances in which the nectar of charming songs flows from their lotus-faces, and which are honored by the first danceress—the Goddess herself—who, intoxicated with joy, rises up to meet them through the gestures of her waving arms, the placement of her feet, and her expressive glances. (37)

Manifesting an indescribable clarity of notes through their proper placement, the sweet sound of the lute—its rhythmic sequence uninterrupted, tasting like nectar within the auspicious [Goddess’s] ear, delightful with various melodies, interwoven with hymns sweet with the nine rasas, and exceedingly charming—is the ear-ornament of the Great Sage [Nārada], whose ears are as long as his body.
It instantly bestows joy upon the hearts of living beings, harmonizing with the beautiful, shimmering golden cymbals resounded by the pair of hands of the celestial nymphs. (38)
May Mārjanā, born from the *maṇi-muraja* (the jeweled drum), purify our dullness—she who causes the peahen to cry out with her own call, which is as skillful as the sound of a drum heavy with water.
To the gods, the demons, the ancestors, the assembly of sages, the Siddhas and Vidyādharas, the Sādhyas and Cāraṇas, to humans, beasts, insects, and even the lowest of species;
and to all those things growing upon the glorious Kailāsa, from blades of grass to shrubs and trees—to all these who take refuge at the feet of Śarva, I offer unhesitating salutation.
Thus meditating, whoever recites this hymn every day at dawn—what more can we say of their virtuous conduct? Or rather, let us describe it in brief:

having attained complete success, high esteem in assemblies, and the affection of all people, they reach the state of the Supreme Brahman, the Enemy of Manmatha, at the end of a hundred years of life.
(41) Thus ends [the work] of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājakācārya...
In the work of the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, the disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda,
the *Śivapādādikeśāntastuti* (Hymn to Śiva from His Feet to the Tip of His Hair) is complete.
